## Repeatability and credibility {#credibility-is-not-truth}

::: {.scaled style="--fs: 0.9; --lh: 1.15"}
"**Repeatability** is used when referring to reproducibility, robustness, and replicability as a constellation of concepts intended to assess whether answers to scientific questions are unchanged when different steps of the research process are repeated."

**Credibility** and **trustworthiness** refer to the confidence one can have in research findings. Because scientific knowledge claims are tentative, they are *not* synonymous with truth.

"For example, credibility is advanced by addressing potential competing interests in the conducting and reporting of research, by taking existing knowledge into account, by using methods that have been validated, by controlling for biases in the research context, by pursuing precise and reliable evidence, and by calibrating the strength of the claims to the uncertainty of the evidence."
:::

::: {.src}
@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms [p. 2]
:::

::: notes
The glossary on this slide is worth reading slowly, because it separates two things we routinely run together. Repeatability is the umbrella: reproducibility, robustness and replicability as a family, all asking whether the answer survives repeating some step of the process. Credibility and trustworthiness are about how much confidence a finding deserves – and note the sentence in the middle. Because scientific claims are tentative, credibility is not the same as truth. A credible finding can be wrong. What credibility is built from is the list at the bottom: declared interests, validated methods, precise evidence, and claims calibrated to the uncertainty behind them. That last one is the one we will keep coming back to.
:::

## Quick check – the matrix in peer review {#quick-check-credibility-in-the-wild .questionslide transition="fade-in none-out"}

::: {.none}
You submit your paper and replication package. It goes out to reviewers.

- 'Reviewer 1' wants to ensure that your results are [reproducible]{.fragment .bounceIn}, so she sources your R script to run the entire analysis. You're in luck – she hasn't yet updated her `dplyr`, so the code runs.
- 'Reviewer 2' is very eager. He's unconvinced by your modelling choices, so he fits your data to another function to check if your findings are truly [robust]{.fragment .bounceIn}. You're in luck again – he recovers your point estimate to a reasonable precision, although the confidence intervals have widened.
- 'Reviewer 3' takes a special interest because he's just working on a similar paper on data they published recently. Do your results [replicate]{.fragment .bounceIn} when your methods are applied to that state-of-the-art dataset?
:::

::: notes
Here is the matrix at work on one paper. You submit a paper with its replication package, and three reviewers each check something different. For each one, call out or type in the chat which cell of the matrix that reviewer is in, before the answer appears. Reviewer 1 reruns your own script on your own data. [pause] [advance] Reproduction. Reviewer 2 fits your data with a different function. [pause] [advance] Robustness. Reviewer 3 applies your methods to a dataset that somebody else published. [pause] [advance] Replication.
:::

## Quick check – the matrix in peer review {#quick-check-credibility-in-the-wild-1 .questionslide transition="none-in fade-out"}

::: {.none}
You submit your paper and replication package. It goes out to reviewers.

'Reviewer 2' just doesn't want to let go...

- He tried a few alternative analyses of your data, including a fancy new regression method that he just released as an R package. His method gives results that are generally aligned to yours, but for the method to work, it would require a larger dataset; would your results really [generalise]{.fragment .bounceIn} to this new dataset published by 'Reviewer 3' that he just read about, if applying his new fancy method to it?
:::

::: notes
Reviewer 2 has not finished. His new method agrees with your results, but it needs more data than you had, so he wants to run it on the dataset that Reviewer 3 published. Which cell is that? [pause] [advance] New data and a new analysis at once put him in the fourth cell, generalisation. Each of these checks asks a different question of the same paper, and passing one of them does not settle the others.
:::

## Open research: the practices {.smaller}

::: {.small}
| Practice | What it makes possible |
|---|---|
| **Open data** | Someone else can re-analyse your evidence |
| **Open code** | Someone else can rerun your exact analysis |
| **Open materials** | Someone else can run your study again |
| **Open access** | Someone else can read the claim in the first place |
| **Preregistration** | A dated record of the analysis plan, filed in a registry before the results exist |
| **Registered reports** | Peer review of the plan, with publication decided before results |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Each one removes a specific obstacle, and none of them guards against every problem. The programme, set out at length: [@MunafoEtAl2017ManifestoReproducibleScience]
:::

::: notes
Each of those reviewers needed something from you before they could start – your code, your data, your materials. Open research is a list of practices that supply those things and more, each of which removes a specific, identifiable obstacle. Open data means someone else can re-analyse your evidence rather than taking your word for it. Open code means they can rerun your exact analysis. Open materials means they can run the study again in a new sample. Open access means they can read the thing at all, which sounds trivial until you try to get a paper from outside a wealthy university. Preregistration produces a dated record of the analysis plan, filed in a registry before the results exist. And registered reports go further: the plan is peer-reviewed and the publication decision is made before anyone sees a result, which removes the incentive to find something. Each removes one obstacle, and none of them guards against every problem. Whether published findings hold up when somebody does check them has now been measured on a large scale.
:::

## The two Multi100 tasks {#two-tasks-months-apart .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 1 – free reanalysis.** Reanalyse the claim however you see fit. Record one categorical conclusion: does the evidence support it?

::: {.fragment}
**Task 2 – constrained reanalysis.** Once Task 1 was in, four instructions arrived, quoted from my own Task 2 report:

> - produce a single, main result in terms of statistical families of z-, t-, F-, or $\chi^2$ tests (or their alternative or non-parametric versions).
> - disregard contextual variables related to the EU policies and party EU salience and party EU positions indexes in your analysis.
> - use the **positive non-materialist form of EU framing** in your analysis.
> - use the **unemployment rate** as the measure for poor economic performance in your analysis.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Task 1 measures whether we agree. Task 2 makes our *numbers* comparable – you cannot average five answers to five different questions.
:::

::: notes
The study ran in two stages, and the distinction matters for everything that follows. Task one was complete freedom: reanalyse the claim however you see fit, and record one categorical conclusion on whether the evidence supports it or not. Once that was submitted, task two arrived with four instructions, and these are the words in which I received them, copied from my own report. Produce a single main result, as a z, t, F or chi-squared test. Disregard the contextual variables that concern EU policies and the salience of the EU and its position for the parties. Use the positive non-materialist form of EU framing, which is the cosmopolitan scale of the paper. And use the unemployment rate as the measure of poor economic performance. The order matters because the two tasks measure different things. Task one asks whether independent analysts reach the same verdict. Task two asks whether they produce the same number, and that second question can only be asked once everyone is answering the same question, which is what the instructions were for.
:::

## Results on a common scale {#how-a-hundred-studies-become-one-number .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Every analyst reports their test statistic and its degrees of freedom, in whatever form their model produces – **t**, **z**, **F**, $\chi^2$
- Each is converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a standardised **Cohen's *d***, so a fixed-effects model fitted in Stata and a multilevel model fitted in R can be read on the same axis
- A **peer panel** judges whether each pipeline is an appropriate analysis of the claim
- Only then can you ask: how far apart are five defensible answers?
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Standardising makes the comparison possible, but it assumes that the five are estimating **the same quantity**, and that the degrees of freedom behind each conversion count the units that carry the evidence. Hold both thoughts.
:::

::: notes
Even with the question pinned down, the answers arrive in different forms. Everyone reports the test statistic that their model happens to produce, with its degrees of freedom – a t, a z, an F, a chi-squared. Those get converted onto a common scale, a partial correlation and a standardised mean difference, so that somebody's fixed-effects model in Stata and somebody else's multilevel model in R can be placed on the same axis and read against each other. Alongside that, a peer panel judged whether each pipeline was an appropriate analysis of the claim at all, so the spread you are about to see is a spread among analyses that passed review. Putting five numbers on one axis takes two things for granted. One is that they estimate the same quantity, and much of the argument about estimands later is about what happens when they do not. The other is that the degrees of freedom fed into each conversion count the units that carry the evidence, and the next chart shows what happens when they do not.
:::

## Open-source software {#what-open-source-buys-you .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **You can read it.** The source of `lm()`, of `feols()`, of every package that this course loads, is public, so no estimator has to be taken on trust
- **No licence stands between a reader and your analysis.** Anyone, anywhere, can run your code without buying anything
- **It outlives your institution.** A licence expires when you change job; a package on CRAN does not
- **You can fix it, and so can others.** Bugs get found because thousands of people run the same code on different data
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
With a proprietary toolchain, **the price of reproducing your work falls on your reader**, who has to buy the licence.
:::

::: notes
Stata is proprietary and R is open source, and that difference matters for reproduction. There are four reasons, and only one of them is money. First, you can read it. You can go and look at the source of any function we run in this course, so you never have to take an estimator on trust. Second, and this is the one that bears on our subject, no licence stands between a reader and your analysis. If your replication package needs a licence they do not have, your work is not reproducible for them, however carefully you wrote it. Third, it outlives your institution – a site licence ends when you change job, and a package on CRAN does not. Fourth, bugs get found, because thousands of people run the same code against different data. On money, the question is who pays. Reproducibility has a price, and a proprietary toolchain hands that price to your reader.
:::

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3|5|7"}
x <- 42                          # <- assigns. "x gets 42"

mean(c(2, 4, 6))                 # a function: name, then arguments in ()

euframes$unemp                   # $ picks one column out of a data frame
```

::: notes
If you have never written a line of R, this slide is most of what you need to read the rest. Four things. First, the arrow assigns: x gets forty-two. You will see the equals sign used the same way and both work, but the arrow is the convention and it reads better out loud. Second, a function is a name followed by round brackets containing its arguments – mean of two, four and six. Third, the dollar sign reaches inside an object to pull out one column. And fourth, the pipe, which is the one that changes how the code reads: it takes whatever is on its left and feeds it in as the first argument of whatever is on its right. So euframes pipe nrow means "take euframes, and count its rows". Once you see the pipe as the word 'then', long chains become readable sentences.

## Model formulas {#a-model-is-a-formula-plus-data .smaller .deepdive run="r"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3|5"}

m <- lm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = euframes)

summary(m)
```

::: {.small}
The tilde `~` reads **outcome on the left, predictors on the right**. Add predictors with `+`. The formula is an object in its own right and is not tied to the function that will eventually use it.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Almost every modelling function in R takes this same shape: `something(formula, data = ...)`. Learn the pattern once and `lm`, `glm`, `lmer`, `feols` and `betareg` all become variations.
:::

::: notes
A model in R is a formula plus data, and the tilde is the heart of the formula: outcome on the left, predictors on the right, and you add more predictors with a plus. The thing that surprises people coming from other software is that the formula is an object in its own right – you can store it in a variable, print it, pass it around – and it is not tied to the function that will eventually use it. Then lm fits a linear model given that formula and a data frame, the arrow names the result, and summary prints the coefficient table. The genuinely useful pattern is on the fragment: almost every modelling function in R has this same shape, something bracket formula comma data. Learn it once and lm, glm, lmer for multilevel models, feols for fixed effects and betareg for bounded outcomes all become variations on one thing you already know.

## Fixed effects with fixest {#fixed-effects-the-fast-way .smaller .deepdive run="r"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|2"}
m1 <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year,
                    data = euframes, vcov = "iid")
```

::: {.small}
The bar `|` separates the regression from the **fixed effects**. Everything after it is absorbed: `cntry` gives every country its own intercept, `year` gives every year its own. `vcov = "iid"` asks for conventional standard errors, the kind on record for this result.

The equivalent with dummies would be `mcosmo ~ unemp_c + factor(cntry) + factor(year)` – same estimate, 36 extra rows of output you do not want to read.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is the model of C6HJR, one of the three that you can reproduce in Hands-on 3, where it gives **`t = −3.804`**. The model of KQXUE keeps only `| cntry`.
:::

::: notes
This is the line that reproduces my own Multi100 reanalysis, one of the three that you can choose in the third hands-on, so it is worth a slow look. Feols comes from the fixest package and fits linear models with fixed effects very fast. The bar is the key piece of syntax: everything to the left of it is the regression, everything to the right is absorbed as fixed effects. Country gives every country its own intercept, so we are comparing each country with itself over time rather than comparing countries with each other. Year gives every year its own intercept, so anything that hit all of Europe in a given year is soaked up. You could write the same model with dummy variables – the estimate would be identical – but you would get thirty-six extra rows of output that nobody wants to read. The last argument, vcov equals iid, asks for conventional standard errors, the kind used for the recorded value. And in the third hands-on this same line gives a t of minus three point eight zero four, while the model of KQXUE drops the year from the right of the bar.
:::

The standard error says how much that estimate would move across repeated samples. The t is the estimate divided by its standard error, here on 233 degrees of freedom, which you can read as how many standard errors the estimate is from zero. And the p-value says how often you would get a t that large if the true value were zero. These are conventional errors, which treat every country-year as an independent observation, and in Part 3 we see what changes when the years of one country are allowed to resemble each other. Now the fragment. Model parameters hands the table back as a data frame. That means you can filter it, join it, stack hundreds of them and plot the lot – and that is how eight hundred and sixty-four specifications become one chart when we reach the multiverse.

## Causal graphs in R {#a-causal-graph-is-a-set-of-formulas .smaller .deepdive run="r"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1-4|2|3|6|7"}
dag <- ggdag::dagify(
  framing ~ unemployment,          # unemployment -> framing
  framing ~ country + year,        # country and year -> framing
  unemployment ~ country + year,   # ... and -> unemployment
  exposure = "unemployment",
  outcome  = "framing")

dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag)                # what must I control for?
```

::: {.small}
Each line is **one arrow, read outcome-first**, following the same convention as a model formula. Because every arrow has its own line, you can comment one out with a `#` and the code still runs.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
`adjustmentSets()` returns the variables that close every back-door path in the graph. Change an arrow, rerun, and watch the answer change.
:::

::: notes
The last piece of R is the one you use in the next task. A causal graph in R is a set of formulas, and they follow the same convention you already learned for models: outcome on the left, cause on the right. So the first line says unemployment points at framing. The second says country and year both point at framing. The third says they also both point at unemployment – which makes them common causes, which makes them confounders. Then you declare which node is the exposure and which is the outcome. The lovely part is that each arrow is its own line, so you can put a hash in front of one and the code still runs, and wiring your beliefs into the graph is literally a matter of commenting lines in and out. [advance] And adjustmentSets reads the finished graph and tells you which variables you must control for. Those are the variables that close every back-door path, a term that the causal-graph slides explain. Change an arrow, rerun it, watch the answer change.
:::

## What the instructions assume {#what-those-three-instructions-assume .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **'A single, main result'** assumes that one test statistic can stand for the claim, and leaves its degrees of freedom to the software of each analyst
- **'The positive non-materialist form'** is the cosmopolitan scale of the paper. It assumes that the five items form one scale, and that the summary used in the paper, each respondent's share of mentions, is the right one; a mean, a sum or a factor score would all be defensible
- **'The unemployment rate'** assumes that the claim is about unemployment. The abstract of the paper says "poor economic performances" – which also names GDP growth
- **'Disregard contextual variables'** of EU policy and party positions removes the variables of Model 2. Read literally, it leaves the rest of Model 1 to the analyst, yet four of the five fitted unemployment alone
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these is wrong. Each one is a **decision**, made for you, that a different study could reasonably have made differently.
:::

::: notes

Asking for a single main result assumes that one test statistic can stand for the claim, and it leaves the degrees of freedom to whatever the software of each analyst reports, which is where the conversion went wrong for one of us. ## Repositories, archives and registries {#open-research-infrastructures .smaller}

::: {.small}
| Kind | What it does | Examples |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Data archive** | holds survey data under the terms of their owners, often behind a registration and a licence | GESIS, the UK Data Service, ICPSR |
| **Statistical office** | publishes official series, usually open for reuse with attribution | Eurostat, the World Bank, national offices |
| **Repository** | keeps data, code and documents at a permanent address that can be cited | the OSF, Zenodo, Dataverse |
| **Registry** | files a dated plan that nobody can edit afterwards | OSF Registries, AsPredicted |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Each answers a question that a reader of a paper asks: where the data are and on what terms, where the code is, and what the authors planned before they had a result.
:::

::: notes
The practices of open research need places to live, and four kinds of infrastructure carry most of them. Data archives hold survey data on behalf of the people who collected them, often behind a registration and a licence, and GESIS, which holds the Eurobarometer, is one. Statistical offices publish the official series, such as unemployment, usually under an open licence that asks only for attribution. Repositories keep data, code and documents at a permanent address that can be cited, and the OSF is the one that this case lives on. Registries file a plan with a date on it, so that a reader can check what was intended before the result arrived. [advance] Each of the four answers a question that a careful reader of a paper asks, and the case of the day touches all four.
:::
